lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Revision: adjective order, tag questions, silent-letter spelling and determiners
objectives: Order several adjectives correctly before a noun.
Form tag questions with the right auxiliary, pronoun and polarity.
Apply the special patterns for tags with I am, let us, imperatives, negative-meaning subjects and nationalities.
Spell asthma and other words with silent letters, and form the related adjective.
Choose determiners according to definiteness, countability and number.
Answer a keyed mixed revision set and explain each correction.
lessons.body:
This is a revision set on four skills tested by the five Week 5 revision questions: adjective order, tag questions (two items), the spelling of a medical word and the choice of a determiner. The source gives no key, its instruction names four options although each item offers five, and one item’s options are merged in the original text. Those items also test skills that the Week 5 teaching does not cover, so this lesson is labelled as revision and does not claim to assess the Week 5 scheme objectives. No answer is inferred from the source’s options; every sentence and answer below is newly written.
English usually arranges several adjectives in this order: determiner, opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, purpose, then the noun. A worked example is ‘a lovely small old round brown wooden writing desk’, where lovely is opinion, small is size, old is age, round is shape, brown is colour, wooden is material and writing is purpose. The purpose slot is often filled by a noun used as an adjective, as in ‘sports shoes’ or ‘kitchen table’. In practice, three adjectives are usually enough; a long string sounds artificial even when the order is correct.
Two order traps matter most. First, age comes before colour, and colour before origin: ‘a new green French bicycle’, not ‘a green new French bicycle’. Second, opinion comes before every fact adjective: ‘a beautiful large round table’, not ‘a large beautiful round table’. Material and purpose come last: ‘a red Italian sports car’. Use a comma between adjectives when they are coordinate, that is, when you could put and between them or reverse their order without changing the sense; do not put a comma between the last adjective and the noun. When you are unsure, build the phrase backwards from the noun and place the most identifying adjective nearest to it.
A tag question is a short question added to a statement. Form it from the auxiliary or modal in the statement, then the pronoun that matches the subject, with the polarity reversed: a positive statement takes a negative tag, and a negative statement takes a positive tag. If the statement has no auxiliary, use do, does or did in the tense of the main verb. ‘The pupils have finished the test, haven’t they?’ matches have with they and reverses the polarity. ‘She does not like crowds, does she?’ reverses the negative. ‘You can swim, can’t you?’ repeats the modal. ‘The boys arrived late, didn’t they?’ supplies did for the past tense.
Several special cases are worth learning as patterns. With I am, the negative tag is aren’t I. With let us, the tag is shall we. An imperative takes will you or won’t you. A statement containing nobody, nothing, never or hardly is negative in meaning, so it takes a positive tag: ‘Nobody called, did they?’ A demonstrative subject becomes it or they: ‘This is yours, isn’t it?’ A person described by nationality or occupation takes he or she: ‘The new coach is a Brazilian, isn’t she?’ When the same word names a language or a country as a thing, the pronoun is it: ‘French is difficult, isn’t it?’ Used to takes didn’t, and have to takes don’t or doesn’t.
The medical word is spelt asthma: a-s-t-h-m-a. The letters th are not pronounced, which is why the spelling is often reduced to asma or given an extra letter. Learn the word with its family: asthma, an asthma attack, and the adjective asthmatic. Many English words carry silent letters for historical reasons, such as the h in rhythm, the b in subtle and doubt, and the n in solemn. Learn such words by syllable and by family rather than by sound alone, and check the silent letter when you write. A dictionary that shows the pronunciation will confirm which letters are not spoken.
Determiners tell the reader how a noun is identified. Use the when the noun is specific, already known or defined by a phrase that follows: ‘She has the right to appeal’, where the phrase to appeal identifies which right. Use a or an for one unspecified member of a class, with an before a vowel sound: ‘He is an honest man’. Use no article for general plurals and uncountables: ‘Pupils need practice’. Use some in statements and offers, and any in negatives and questions. Use each for members considered one by one, including two: ‘Each of the two answers is correct’. Use every for three or more considered as a group; every cannot be followed by of the.
In an examination, read the whole sentence before you look at the options, and name the skill being tested. For adjective order, build the phrase from the noun backwards. For a tag question, find the auxiliary, the tense and the pronoun, then reverse the polarity. For a spelling, recall the word family and the silent letter. For a determiner, ask whether the noun is specific or general, countable or uncountable, and whether the choice depends on a following phrase. Substitute your answer into the sentence and read it aloud silently. If one option is garbled or missing, mark the item and return to it; do not let it cost you the other questions.
The Week 5 source set has five items but no key, and its rubric promises four options while each item supplies five. One item’s options run together in the original text, so it cannot be answered from the printed choices; this lesson does not repair or copy it. The set also tests adjective order, tag questions, spelling and determiners, none of which the Week 5 teaching covers, and it asks two tag questions rather than balancing the skills. The keyed items below are new sentences on the same four skills, with a worked answer for every item. The source is not edited, and no answer is taken from its options.

practice.question: Put the adjectives in the correct order before the noun. (a) a [wooden / small / old] box. (b) a [French / new / green] bicycle. (c) a [round / beautiful / large] table. (d) [sports / Italian / red] shoes. (e) an [interesting / old / Nigerian] novel.
practice.answer: (a) a small old wooden box: size, age, material. (b) a new green French bicycle: age, colour, origin. (c) a beautiful large round table: opinion, size, shape. (d) red Italian sports shoes: colour, origin, purpose. (e) an interesting old Nigerian novel: opinion, age, origin.

practice.question: Add the correct question tag. (a) The pupils have finished the test, ___? (b) She does not like crowds, ___? (c) You can swim, ___? (d) Let us begin, ___? (e) Nobody called while I was out, ___? (f) I am late, ___?
practice.answer: (a) haven’t they: have matches the auxiliary and they matches the pupils. (b) does she: the negative statement takes a positive tag. (c) can’t you: can is repeated and you matches. (d) shall we: let us takes shall we. (e) did they: nobody is negative in meaning, so the tag is positive. (f) aren’t I: the special tag for I am.

practice.question: Spell the missing word in each item. (a) The nurse treated a child with ___, a condition that makes breathing difficult. (b) The drummer kept a steady ___ throughout the song. (c) The difference is ___ and easy to miss. (d) The hall fell ___ when the head teacher entered. (e) Write the adjective formed from the word in (a).
practice.answer: (a) asthma: a-s-t-h-m-a, with silent th. (b) rhythm: r-h-y-t-h-m, with silent h. (c) subtle: s-u-b-t-l-e, with silent b. (d) solemn: s-o-l-e-m-n, with silent n. (e) asthmatic: a-s-t-h-m-a-t-i-c.

practice.question: Choose the correct determiner and explain the choice. (a) She has ___ right to appeal. (a / the / any) (b) ___ of the two answers is correct. (Every / Each / Some) (c) I need ___ information about the trip. (an / some / every) (d) He is ___ honest man. (a / an / the)
practice.answer: (a) the: the phrase to appeal identifies a specific right. (b) Each: each is used for members considered one by one, including two; every needs three or more and cannot take of. (c) some: information is uncountable and this is a request. (d) an: honest begins with a vowel sound, although it begins with the letter h.

practice.question: Each item offers four options, A to D. Select the option that best completes the sentence. (1) That ___ belongs to my aunt. A old blue Japanese vase B blue old Japanese vase C Japanese old blue vase D old Japanese blue vase. (2) The children are ready, ___? A aren’t they B isn’t it C don’t they D are they. (3) He has ___ unusual hobby. A a B an C the D some. (4) The word for a serious breathing condition is spelt A asma B astma C asthma D asmah. (5) You have met my brother, ___? A haven’t you B didn’t you C don’t you D have you.
practice.answer: (1) A old blue Japanese vase: age, colour, origin. (2) A aren’t they: are matches and they replaces the children. (3) B an: unusual begins with a vowel sound. (4) C asthma. (5) A haven’t you: have matches and you is the subject.

practice.question: Each sentence is faulty. Correct it and name the fault. (a) a green new French car. (b) She can drive, can she? (c) The new coach is a Brazilian, isn’t it? (d) every of the pupils was present. (e) a beautiful wooden small box.
practice.answer: (a) a new green French car: age comes before colour and origin. (b) She can drive, can’t she?: the positive statement needs a negative tag. (c) The new coach is a Brazilian, isn’t she?: a person described by nationality takes she. (d) each of the pupils was present: every cannot be followed by of the; each can. (e) a beautiful small wooden box: opinion comes first and material comes last.

marking.criterion: (e) corrected order with opinion first and material last

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Figures of speech: simile, metaphor, personification, irony and the rhetorical question
objectives: Define a figure of speech and separate figures that work by comparison, by contrast and by the form of a question.
Define simile and metaphor, tell them apart by form and reject plain comparisons and literal uses of is.
Define personification and identify a non-human thing given a human act or feeling.
Define verbal and situational irony and use the context to establish the intended contrast.
Define the rhetorical question and tell it from a real question.
Identify a figure, explain its effect and write an original example of each figure, with a keyed, marked exercise.
lessons.body:
A figure of speech is a deliberate use of words that departs from their plain, literal sense in order to create an effect that a literal statement could not: a clearer picture, stronger feeling, emphasis, humour or persuasion. Figures of speech do not all work in the same way. Simile, metaphor and personification work by comparison. Irony works by contrast, between what is said and what is meant or expected. The rhetorical question works by form: it is a question asked for effect and not for an answer. A writer who says “The room was cold” is being literal; a writer who says “The room was a freezer” is using a figure, because the room is not really a freezer and the reader must see the idea behind the picture. The test is always the same: ask whether the literal sense fits the situation, and if it does not, name the figure, state the idea the writer intends and say what effect it has. Reading this lesson with the earlier lesson on literal and figurative meaning will help, but the five figures below are taught here in full.
Simile. A simile is an openly stated comparison between two things of different kinds, introduced by like or as (or as … as). “The rain fell on the zinc roof like thrown pebbles” compares rain with pebbles; “Chinedu was as quiet as a stone during the quarrel” compares a person with a stone. Two conditions must be met. First, the comparison must be marked by like or as. Second, the two things must be unlike: “My sister sings like our mother” compares two singers and is plain comparison, not a simile, whereas “Her voice rang like a bell” compares a voice with an object. The effect of a simile is to let the reader borrow a quality from something familiar: the pebbles give the sound of the rain a hard, scattered quality; the stone gives Chinedu’s silence a heavy, unmoving quality.
Metaphor. A metaphor is an implied comparison: it speaks of one thing as if it were another and does not use like or as. “The library was a quiet island in the middle of the noisy school” does not say that the library resembles an island; it calls it one, so that the reader carries over the ideas of calm, separation and shelter. “Ngozi is the backbone of our team” carries over the idea of support on which everything else depends. The difference from a simile is therefore one of form: “The road was like a ribbon” is a simile; “The road was a ribbon” is a metaphor. A metaphor can also work through a verb or adjective: in “Questions rained on the speaker”, questions are said to rain. Take care, because the word is does not make a sentence a metaphor. “Lagos is a large city” is literal, since Lagos really is a city; the sentence is a metaphor only when the two things are of different kinds and the statement cannot be literally true.
Personification. Personification gives human actions, feelings or qualities to something that is not human: an animal, an object, a place, a force of nature or an idea. “The old generator groaned and refused to wake up” makes a machine groan and refuse, which are human acts. “Fear crept into the room and sat beside her” makes an idea creep and sit. The test is that a non-human thing does something only a person does. “The dog barked” is literal, because dogs bark; “The dog smiled politely at the visitor” gives the dog a human manner and is personification. The effect is to make the thing seem alive and to make the reader feel towards it as towards a person: the generator becomes a tired, stubborn old man; fear becomes an unwelcome guest.
Irony. In irony there is a contrast between what appears and what is true, and the reader can see it only if the situation is known. In verbal irony a speaker or writer says one thing and means the opposite. Context makes the contrast clear. Suppose a cook leaves the rice to burn and the stew to boil dry, and her brother looks at the blackened pot and says, “What a wonderful meal you have prepared.” The words praise the meal, but everyone can see that the meal is ruined, so the real meaning is the opposite of the words: it is a failure. Verbal irony that is meant to hurt or mock is called sarcasm. In situational irony the contrast lies in events: what happens is the opposite of what was expected or intended. A school holds an anti-litter campaign, and the field is covered in litter after the closing party. Nobody speaks ironically, but the outcome contradicts the purpose. Irony is not the same as bad luck or coincidence: a farmer whose crops are destroyed by a flood has suffered a misfortune, and it is irony only if the outcome contradicts something that was said or intended, as when he has just boasted that his land can never flood. Without the context, a line such as “What a wonderful meal” could be sincere, so an answer about irony must always name the context that shows the contrast.
Rhetorical question. A rhetorical question is a question asked to make a point, not to get information. The speaker expects either no answer or one answer that everybody already holds, and the audience supplies it silently. “Who would choose to sit in the dark when the switch is beside him?” does not ask for a name; it states that nobody would. A councillor who says to a town meeting, “Do we want our river to become a rubbish dump?” is not waiting for a reply; she means that we do not, and she expects the audience to agree. The effect is emphasis and persuasion: the statement comes as a challenge, and the listener becomes a partner in the argument. A question is not rhetorical simply because the speaker knows the answer. A teacher who asks, “What is a simile?” wants a pupil to answer, so the question is a real one. It is rhetorical only when no answer is wanted.
Identifying a figure and explaining its effect. Work through the sentence in order. If there is a comparison marked by like or as between unlike things, it is a simile. If one thing is called another, or described in terms of another, with no like or as, it is a metaphor. If a non-human thing acts or feels as a person does, it is personification. If the words or events contradict the real situation, which you must establish from the context, it is irony. If it is a question that wants no answer, it is a rhetorical question. A sentence may contain more than one figure: in “The wind whispered through the hall like a secret” the wind is made to whisper (personification) and is compared with a secret (simile). When you explain an effect, do not stop at the name of the figure; state what picture or feeling the reader receives. “It is a simile” is a label, not an explanation. “It compares the queue with a snail, so the reader pictures a very slow line and shares the impatience of the people in it” is an explanation. Use figures sparingly, because a figure in every line tires the reader and weakens each one.

practice.question: Name the figure of speech in each sentence and give one reason. (a) “The new teacher’s voice was as soft as cotton wool.” (b) “The classroom was a beehive during the break.” (c) “The kettle sang happily on the stove.” (d) Obi forgot his keys, missed the bus and spilled his tea. “What a perfect start to the day,” he sighed. (e) A head cook warns the kitchen helpers: “Who would leave a pot on the fire and walk away?”
practice.answer: (a) Simile: the teacher’s voice is compared with cotton wool, two unlike things, and the comparison is marked by as … as. (b) Metaphor: the classroom is called a beehive with no like or as, and it cannot literally be one; the idea carried over is crowded, noisy activity. (c) Personification: a kettle is given a human act and feeling (singing happily). (d) Irony (verbal irony or sarcasm): Obi says the day has started perfectly, but the context shows that it has started badly, so he means the opposite of what he says. (e) Rhetorical question: the cook wants no answer; she means that nobody should do it.

marking.criterion: (a) simile, with the like/as marker or the unlike things named
(b) metaphor, with no like or as or the implied comparison named
(c) personification, with the human act or feeling named
(d) irony, with the contrast between the words and the bad morning named
(e) rhetorical question, with the idea that no answer is wanted

practice.question: Explain the effect of each sentence. (a) “The queue moved like a snail.” (b) At a town meeting about factory waste, a councillor says, “Do we want our river to become a rubbish dump?”
practice.answer: (a) It is a simile. It compares the queue with a snail, so the reader pictures a very slow, creeping line and shares the impatience of the people in it. (b) It is a rhetorical question. The councillor wants no reply: she means that we do not want it, and she expects the audience to agree silently. The effect is emphasis and persuasion, because it makes the listeners join her view and treat pollution as something they must refuse.

marking.criterion: (a) states what is compared (queue and snail)
(a) states the effect: slowness and impatience
(b) states the effect: emphasis or persuasion

practice.question: Read this. Amaka spent weeks telling everyone that she would never be late again. On the day of the prize-giving for punctuality, she arrived after the last speech. “Congratulations on your punctuality prize,” said her friend, smiling. (a) What do the friend’s words say literally? (b) What does the friend really mean? (c) Which detail in the story shows the contrast? (d) Name the kind of irony in the friend’s words. (e) Name one event that is situational irony.
practice.answer: (a) The words say that Amaka deserves a prize for being on time. (b) She means that Amaka was late, so she does not deserve it, and perhaps that she is being teased. (c) Amaka arrived after the last speech, at the very ceremony that honours punctuality. (d) Verbal irony (sarcasm). (e) Amaka, who promised never to be late, was late for the punctuality prize-giving, so the outcome contradicts her promise and the occasion.

marking.criterion: (b) intended meaning stated as the opposite
(c) arriving after the last speech, or the contradiction with her promise

practice.question: Write one original example of each: (a) a simile, (b) a metaphor, (c) a personification, (d) a rhetorical question, (e) irony, with a sentence of context that makes the intended contrast clear.
practice.answer: Model answers; any correct original example is accepted. (a) “The tired boy fell asleep as quickly as a light going out.” (b) “The market was a river of colour.” (c) “The sun peeped over the hill and greeted the farmers.” (d) “Can we call ourselves a clean town when our gutters are full of rubbish?” (e) Context: Tunde had practised all week and then froze on stage, forgetting every line. His coach said, “That was a flawless performance.” Acceptable criteria: (a) has like or as and compares unlike things; (b) calls one thing another with no like or as and cannot be literally true; (c) gives a non-human thing a human act or feeling; (d) is a question that expects no answer or the obvious one; (e) has context that shows what is expected or true and a statement or outcome that contradicts it. Mark 1 for the figure formed correctly and 1 for clarity (not ambiguous, not copied from this lesson).

marking.criterion: (e) irony formed correctly, with a contradiction

practice.question: Correct each statement. (a) “Every sentence with the word is in it is a metaphor.” (b) “A simile compares two things of the same kind.” (c) “Irony means any sad or unlucky event.”
practice.answer: (a) Wrong. Is does not make a metaphor. “Lagos is a large city” is literal; a metaphor calls one thing another of a different kind, so that the statement cannot be literally true, as in “The library was an island.” (b) Wrong. A simile compares two unlike things, marked by like or as. “She sings like her mother” is a plain comparison. (c) Wrong. Irony is a contrast between what is said or expected and what is true or what happens. A misfortune is irony only if it contradicts an expectation, a statement or an intention.

marking.criterion: (a) rejects the claim and gives a literal is example or the true test
(b) says unlike things and like or as
(c) says contrast or contradiction of an expectation

practice.question: In “The wind whispered through the hall like a secret”, name the two figures of speech, quote the words that show each and explain the effect of the sentence.
practice.answer: Personification: “whispered”, because wind is given a human act. Simile: “like a secret”, because the wind is compared with a secret and the comparison is marked by like. Effect: the reader hears a soft, low, mysterious sound and feels that the hall is quiet and slightly eerie.

marking.criterion: effect: soft, mysterious or eerie sound or mood

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: The descriptive essay: scope, dominant impression, sensory detail and organisation
objectives: State the scope of a descriptive essay (an object, person, animal, incident or scene) and tell a descriptive task from a narrative one.
Choose a dominant impression and select only the details that build it.
Use sensory detail, precise words and sparing comparison to show rather than label a feeling.
Organise a descriptive essay with an introduction, focused paragraphs in one kept order and a conclusion, using a worked plan for ‘A rainy day I will live to remember’.
Write and mark a short descriptive paragraph on that title against a five-feature marking guide, with a model response.
lessons.body:
A descriptive essay builds a picture in words. Its subject can be an object, a person, an animal, an incident or a scene, and its task word is usually describe. To describe is to show what the subject is like to see, hear, smell, touch and feel, so that the reader can almost step into it. This is different from a narrative essay, which tells what happened next and how it ended. A descriptive essay may still be about an incident, such as a storm or a market fire, but it treats the incident as a scene to be looked at slowly and not as a plot to be moved through. Scope means deciding how much to cover. A good descriptive essay does not try to say everything about its subject; it takes one clear view of it and stays there. Every person, place and event used as an example in this lesson is invented for practice.
Choose a dominant impression before you write. The dominant impression is the one main effect you want the reader to be left with, for example that a market at noon is deafening, that a village at night is peaceful or that a flooded road is frightening. It works like a filter. For every detail you think of, ask whether it builds the impression. If the impression is ‘deafening’, then a loudspeaker blaring, traders shouting prices and engines honking all belong, while a goat sleeping quietly under a table does not, however true it may be. Leave out details that pull against the impression or that add nothing to it. A reader finishes a good description able to say, in one word or phrase, what the place or experience was like.
Build the impression from sensory detail. The five senses are sight, sound, smell, touch and taste, and a strong description uses at least three of them, choosing the ones that fit the scene. Show the reader the detail and do not simply name the feeling. ‘The rain was frightening’ labels a feeling and proves nothing; ‘The rain hammered the zinc roof so hard that I could not hear my own voice’ lets the reader hear it. Prefer precise nouns and strong verbs to piles of adjectives: ‘water raced along the gutters’ is stronger than ‘there was a lot of very fast water’. One well-chosen simile or metaphor can carry an impression, as the lesson on figures of speech shows, but a comparison in every sentence tires the reader and hides the real detail. The Week 3 essay-types lesson gives a short plan for a descriptive essay; this lesson extends it with scope, a worked plan, a model paragraph and a marking guide.
Organise the details so that the reader can follow them. Use the usual three-part frame. The introduction names the subject and gives the dominant impression, without opening with ‘My name is’ or a dictionary definition. The body has two to four paragraphs, and each paragraph has one focus, such as a time of day, a place or a sense. The conclusion closes with the lasting impression and adds no new scene. Choose one principle of order and keep it: spatial order moves from near to far or from the gate to the courtyard; time order moves from morning to evening; order of importance moves from the quietest detail to the most striking one. Time order suits a day, but in a descriptive essay each stage is a picture and not a step in a story. If you find yourself writing ‘then I ran’ and ‘next he said’, you have drifted into narration. For a day that you remember, use the past tense throughout.
Read the title carefully. ‘A rainy day I will live to remember’ names one particular day, makes rain its central subject and says the day matters because it stays in the memory. That points to a dominant impression that you could still feel years later, such as awe at the downpour, the hush that came over a crowded place or the strange peace of a town that slowed down. Ask four questions before you plan. What kind of rain was it: a drizzle, a steady fall or a violent storm? Where were you, and who or what was around you? What did the rain change, whether it brought comfort, trouble or both? What detail will you still remember most clearly? You may set the day in a town, a village, a school or a journey, and you may use real or imagined details, as long as they build one impression. Do not turn the essay into a plot about what you did.
A worked plan for ‘A rainy day I will live to remember’. Dominant impression: the rain made a busy town slow down and fall silent. Paragraph 1, introduction: name the day and state the impression in a single sentence that makes the reader curious. Paragraph 2, early morning: a heavy grey sky, the smell of dust before the first drops, the first fat drops on the roof, a muffled street. Paragraph 3, midday: the downpour at its fiercest, with the drumming on zinc, brown water racing along the gutters, people crowded under shop awnings, cold air on the skin. Paragraph 4, evening: the rain softens, the smell of wet earth rises, lights shine on the wet road, people walk home slowly. Paragraph 5, conclusion: say why the day has stayed in memory, using the lasting impression of the hush and the slowness. The order is time order, and every paragraph is a picture of the same impression.
A model paragraph for paragraph 3 of the plan, original and written to show the features above. “By midday the rain had stopped falling in drops and begun falling in ropes. It drummed on the zinc roof of our classroom so loudly that Mrs Bello gave up the lesson and simply watched the window. Beyond the glass, the football field had become a shallow brown lake, and the goalposts stood in it like the masts of drowned boats. A cold, earthy smell crept under the door, and my damp sleeves clung to my arms. Every few seconds thunder rolled across the sky, and the whole class fell quiet together. Nobody laughed. Nobody moved. For the first time that term, forty restless children simply listened to the sky.” The dominant impression is the power of the storm, which silenced a whole room. The paragraph uses sound, sight, smell and touch, one metaphor (‘ropes’) and one simile, all in the past tense, with details that serve a single impression and no story of what anyone did next.
How the writing task is marked. A descriptive paragraph or essay is marked on five features: dominant impression (4 marks), sensory detail (5), language, meaning precise words and well-chosen comparisons (4), organisation within the paragraph, meaning order, focus and linking (3) and accuracy of grammar, tense and spelling (4). Common faults to avoid are a long list of adjectives with no detail, stray details that pull against the impression, a drift into narrative, mixed tenses and a figure of speech in every line. The same five features can be used to mark a full essay when each is judged across all the paragraphs.

practice.question: Decide whether each task asks for a descriptive essay or a narrative essay, and say which word or phrase in the task tells you. (a) Describe your school hall during morning assembly. (b) Narrate how you got lost on the way to a wedding. (c) Describe a stormy night in your village. (d) Write an account of a quarrel that ended in an apology.
practice.answer: (a) Descriptive: ‘Describe’ asks for a picture of a scene. (b) Narrative: ‘Narrate’ asks for events in sequence. (c) Descriptive: ‘Describe’ asks for a picture of a night scene. (d) Narrative: ‘an account of a quarrel that ended in an apology’ asks for a sequence of events with an ending.

marking.criterion: (a) descriptive, with the task word describe (or a picture of a scene) given as the reason
(b) narrative, with narrate or the sequence of events given as the reason
(c) descriptive, with the task word describe (or a picture of a night scene) given as the reason
(d) narrative, with a quarrel that ended in an apology, meaning a sequence of events with an ending, given as the reason

practice.question: The title is ‘A market at noon’ and the writer wants the dominant impression to be one of noise. Here are six details: (1) a loudspeaker blares music; (2) traders shout their prices; (3) a goat sleeps quietly under a table; (4) lorries honk their horns; (5) buyers clap their hands to close bargains; (6) a blue sign hangs above the gate. State the dominant impression in one word, name the two details that do not build it and say why each does not.
practice.answer: The impression is noise (accept loud, deafening or noisy). Detail (3) does not build it because a goat sleeping quietly is a silent detail that pulls against the impression. Detail (6) does not build it because a sign is only something to see and adds no sound, so it does nothing for the impression of noise.

marking.criterion: Names the impression as noise, loudness or an equivalent word
Reason for (3): it is quiet or silent and pulls against the impression
Reason for (6): it adds no sound or contributes nothing to the impression

practice.question: Rewrite this flat sentence in one or two sentences so that it shows the rain through at least two different senses and uses precise words instead of ‘very heavy’ and ‘bad’: “The rain was very heavy and the road was bad.” Name the two senses you used.
practice.answer: Model answer: “Rain hammered the roofs so loudly that I had to shout, and the road had turned into a brown stream that sucked at my shoes.” Senses used: sound (hammered, shout) and sight (a brown stream), with touch (sucked at my shoes). Any rewrite that uses two or more different senses with precise words is acceptable.

marking.criterion: Uses a first sense through a concrete detail (for example sound)
Uses a second, different sense through a concrete detail (for example sight or touch)
Replaces ‘very heavy’ and ‘bad’ with precise verbs or nouns and does not repeat them
Names correctly the two senses used

practice.question: These plan points for ‘A rainy day I will live to remember’ are in the wrong order. Write the letters in the best order for a descriptive essay in time order. (a) Midday: the downpour at its fiercest, with brown water racing along the gutters. (b) Early morning: a heavy grey sky and the smell of dust before the first drops. (c) Evening: the rain softens, the smell of wet earth rises and lights shine on the road. (d) Conclusion: why the day has stayed in memory. (e) Introduction: names the day and gives the impression that the rain made the town slow down.
practice.answer: e, b, a, c, d. The introduction (e) comes first and the conclusion (d) last. The body follows time order: early morning (b), midday (a), evening (c).

marking.criterion: All three body points lie between (e) and (d) with no point out of place

practice.question: Writing task. Write one descriptive paragraph of 90 to 130 words about the fiercest moment of the rain on ‘A rainy day I will live to remember’. Decide your dominant impression first, use at least three senses, keep the past tense and do not tell a story of what you did next.
practice.answer: Model response (about 120 words; the dominant impression is that the roar of the rain levelled everyone): “The sky split open just as I reached the motor park. Rain hammered the tin roofs so hard that the drivers’ shouting shrank to a distant mumble. Within a minute, brown water raced along the gutters, carrying orange peels and plastic bags like tiny boats. The air turned cold and smelt of hot dust being washed away. I pressed myself against the damp wall of a kiosk while a stranger’s umbrella dripped onto my shoes. Nobody could hear the radio crackling behind the counter, and nobody tried. For those few minutes the roar of the rain was the only sound in the whole motor park, and everyone in it, rich or poor, stood equally wet, small and strangely happy.” Acceptable answers: any paragraph of about 90 to 130 words that keeps one clear dominant impression, uses at least three senses through concrete detail, has precise words, stays in the past tense and does not drift into a plot. Different settings and impressions are acceptable; apply the five features in the marking criteria.

marking.criterion: Dominant impression (max 4): 4 = one impression is clear and every detail serves it; 3 = clear, with one stray detail; 2 = partly clear, with several stray details; 1 = vague; 0 = none
Sensory detail (max 5): 5 = at least three senses, each with concrete detail; 4 = three senses with some vague detail; 3 = two senses; 2 = one sense; 1 = feelings named but not shown; 0 = none
Language (max 4): 4 = precise nouns and verbs and one or two well-chosen comparisons; 3 = mostly precise; 2 = many empty adjectives; 1 = flat or repetitive; 0 = unintelligible
Organisation within the paragraph (max 3): 3 = one focus, a clear order and a closing line; 2 = mostly focused; 1 = loosely ordered or drifts into narrative; 0 = no order
Accuracy (max 4): 4 = few errors and a steady past tense; 3 = some errors that do not hinder meaning; 2 = frequent errors; 1 = errors often hinder meaning; 0 = meaning lost

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: The adverbial clause: definition, subordinators, the eight kinds, punctuation and a keyed exercise
objectives: Define an adverbial clause as a subordinate clause performing the adverbial function, and identify it by the subject-and-finite-verb test inside the group of words.

Name the usual subordinators of each kind - time, place, reason, condition, concession, purpose, result and manner - and classify a clause by the relation it expresses rather than by the isolated word.
Tell an adverbial clause from an adverbial phrase, and tell both from a noun clause, using the question the group answers and the structure inside it.
Punctuate an adverbial clause correctly when it is fronted and when it follows the main clause, and avoid the fragment and the comma splice.
Apply the time rule that a present or perfect form follows a time subordinator, and the unless rule that unless is not used for a contrary-to-fact condition.
Identify, classify, combine and correct adverbial clauses in a keyed, marked exercise.
lessons.body:
An adverbial is a part of a sentence, not a class of word. It is the element that answers a circumstantial question about the clause - when, where, why, how, how often, for how long, on what condition, with what result or despite what. The same job can be done in three different forms: by a single adverb (immediately), by an adverbial phrase (early in the morning) or by an adverbial clause (as soon as the bell rang). An adverbial clause is a subordinate clause that performs the adverbial function of the clause it belongs to. Two tests fix the name. First, look inside the group of words: if it carries its own subject together with a verb that shows tense, it is a clause, so in as soon as the bell rang the bell is the subject and rang is a finite verb. Second, look at the whole group: if it can be moved to the front of the sentence or removed without wrecking the rest, it is an adverbial. The pupils stopped as soon as the bell rang becomes As soon as the bell rang, the pupils stopped, and either version still has a complete main clause. A subordinate clause cannot stand alone as a sentence; written by itself it is a fragment, not a sentence.
The word that introduces the clause is a subordinating conjunction, and it is the first signal of the kind: because marks a reason, although marks a concession, if marks a condition, when marks time, so that marks a purpose. Classify from the relation between the two clauses, never from the isolated word, because several words serve more than one kind and more than one class. Since introduces a reason in Since the road was flooded, we stayed indoors but marks time in She has lived in Ibadan since 2019; as introduces reason, time or manner; that is part of the subordinators so that and provided that but is a relative pronoun after a noun in the book that she borrowed. Ask what question the clause answers and paraphrase the relation, and the kind follows.
Because adverbial names a function while clause names a form, an adverbial clause must be told apart from an adverbial phrase, and the way to do it is to look inside the group rather than at what it tells you. Compare The dancers moved in time with the drum, where in time with the drum has no subject and no finite verb and is therefore a phrase, with The dancers moved as the drum beat, where the drum is a subject and beat is a finite verb, so the group is a clause. The same word can sit in either structure: after dinner is a prepositional phrase, while after we had dined is an adverbial clause, and after is a preposition in the first and a subordinating conjunction in the second. A quick substitution test confirms the answer: replace the group with a single adverb such as then, there or slowly. If one word can do the same job, the group is functioning as an adverbial; whether it is a phrase or a clause is decided by the subject-and-finite-verb test inside it. This lesson teaches the clause only. The scheme objective for Week 10 on adverbial and prepositional phrases is a separate objective and is not treated here, and nothing in this lesson is offered as coverage of it.
Punctuation follows position. When the adverbial clause comes first, a comma normally separates it from the main clause: If the bus is late, we will walk. When it comes after the main clause, the comma is normally unnecessary: We will walk if the bus is late. A clause of reason placed second is often still set off by a comma when the writer wants a pause before the explanation, and a purpose clause with so that usually is, but the rule a marker looks for is the fronted comma. Two errors follow from ignoring the structure. Two main clauses must never be joined by a comma alone: It was raining, we cancelled the trip is a comma splice; make one clause subordinate (Because it was raining, we cancelled the trip) or coordinate them (It was raining, so we cancelled the trip). And a subordinate clause must never be left standing as its own sentence: Because the generators failed twice. is a fragment; attach it to a main clause. Watch the difference between so and so that in those two corrected sentences: so joins two main clauses and is a coordinating conjunction, while so that introduces a subordinate purpose clause and is a subordinating conjunction.
Time and place. An adverbial clause of time answers when, how long or how often, and its common subordinators are when, while, as, before, after, since, until, once and as soon as: When the bell rang, the pupils carried their exercise books to the staff room. Time has one rule that examiners test again and again: after a time subordinator, English uses a present or a perfect form, not will - Write to me when you reach Kaduna, never When you will reach Kaduna. An adverbial clause of place answers where, and its subordinators are where and wherever: Where the path leaves the main road, a broken signpost still points to the health centre. Set the apparatus where every pupil in the back row can see it. Do not call every where-group an adverbial clause: in I know where she lives, the where-group is the object of knows and is a noun clause, while in Sit wherever you like it modifies sit and tells where, so it is an adverbial clause of place.
Reason and purpose. An adverbial clause of reason answers why, and is introduced by because, as, since, now that and seeing that: The practical was cancelled because the laboratory had no water. An adverbial clause of purpose answers why something was done with what end in view, and is introduced by so that, in order that and, in formal or older usage, lest: The teacher repeated the instruction twice so that no pupil would miss it. Keep the two apart by paraphrase. A reason clause explains why the main event happened - this happened, and this is the cause. A purpose clause names an aim the agent was trying to reach - this was done, and this is what it was meant to achieve. The test is whether the second clause could have failed: a purpose can fail (she studied hard but still lost the seat), a stated reason cannot, because if it did not cause the event it was not the reason. A purpose clause normally follows the main clause; bringing it first is formal: So that nobody would miss the instruction, the teacher repeated it twice.
Condition and concession. An adverbial clause of condition states the circumstance on which the main clause depends, with if, unless, provided that, providing that, as long as, so long as and on condition that: If the school bus starts by seven, the team will reach the venue before the practical begins. Unless means if ... not and is used for a real, present or future condition: You will not finish the paper unless you write faster. Do not use unless for a contrary-to-fact condition; if the council had repaired the bridge is not expressed as unless the council had repaired the bridge. An adverbial clause of concession states something that would be expected to prevent the main clause but does not, with although, though, even though, while in its contrast sense, whereas, no matter how and whatever: Although the generators failed twice, the demonstration continued. Condition and concession are distinguished by one question: does the main event happen only if the subordinate one does, or does it happen despite the subordinate one? The first is condition, the second is concession. Whereas and while in this sense contrast two facts, and the comma before the clause is normal when while opens the sentence: While the junior section used the hall, the senior section used the field.
Result and manner. An adverbial clause of result states what followed from a degree already expressed, and is built with so + adjective or adverb + that, and such a (or such + adjective + plural noun) + that: The queue was so long that the bell rang before Tunde reached the desk, and It was such a loud alarm that the whole block emptied in two minutes. The pair is one structure, so in an answer isolate the that-clause but credit the so ... that frame, and never treat so alone as the subordinator here. Result differs from purpose in direction: purpose names what the agent intended before the act, result names what in fact came after it. An adverbial clause of manner answers how or in what way, with as, as if and as though, and informally with the way: The trainee nurse held the bottle as her instructor had shown her. She answered the last question as if she had prepared it beforehand. As if and as though introduce a comparison with an imagined or doubtful state, and a past or subjunctive form after them signals that the speaker does not present the comparison as a fact.
How to work on these in a test. First, find the main clause - the part that could stand alone. Second, take the remaining group of words and apply the inside test: does it have its own subject and a verb showing tense? If yes it is a clause; if it has a preposition with a noun phrase, or only an adverb, it is a phrase and you are answering a different objective. Third, ask the circumstantial question the group answers and paraphrase the relation - when, where, why, on what condition, despite what, with what aim, with what result or in what way - then name the kind. Fourth, punctuate: put a comma after a fronted clause, take it away when the clause follows the main clause, and check that you have not left a fragment or written a comma splice. Worked example. In Although the market road was closed, the traders reached their stalls on foot, the main clause is the traders reached their stalls on foot; although the market road was closed has its own subject, the market road, and a finite verb, was closed, so it is a clause; it is not the condition for reaching the stalls but an obstacle they overcame, so it is concession; and it stands first, so the comma after it is required.

practice.question: Underline the adverbial clause in each sentence and state its kind (time, place, reason, condition, concession, purpose, result or manner). (1) Because the harmattan was severe, the form-two pupils watered the seedlings twice a day. (2) The electrician tested the socket after he had connected the earth wire. (3) Keep the samples where they will not be disturbed. (4) Although the market road was closed, the traders reached their stalls on foot. (5) She lowered her voice so that the class behind her could hear the answer. (6) The trainee nurse held the bottle as her instructor had shown her.
practice.answer: (1) Because the harmattan was severe - reason. (2) after he had connected the earth wire - time. (3) where they will not be disturbed - place. (4) Although the market road was closed - concession. (5) so that the class behind her could hear the answer - purpose. (6) as her instructor had shown her - manner.

marking.criterion: (1) clause located: Because the harmattan was severe
(2) clause located: after he had connected the earth wire
(3) clause located: where they will not be disturbed
(4) clause located: Although the market road was closed
(5) clause located: so that the class behind her could hear the answer
(6) clause located: as her instructor had shown her

practice.question: Say whether the words in capitals are an adverbial CLAUSE or an adverbial PHRASE, and give the structural reason for your answer. (1) The assembly ended BEFORE THE BELL. (2) The assembly ended BEFORE THE BELL RANG. (3) The pupils worked IN SILENCE. (4) The pupils worked AS IF THEY WERE BEING WATCHED.
practice.answer: (1) Phrase - the group has no subject and no finite verb; before takes the noun phrase the bell. (2) Clause - it has the subject the bell and the finite verb rang. (3) Phrase - in silence is a preposition with a noun and contains no verb. (4) Clause - it has the subject they and the finite verb were.

marking.criterion: (1) reason: no subject and no finite verb
(2) reason: subject the bell with finite verb rang
(3) reason: preposition with a noun and no verb
(4) reason: subject they with finite verb were

practice.question: Join the two sentences in each pair into one sentence, using the subordinator given in brackets, and punctuate correctly. (1) The inter-house final will be played. The rain stops by noon. (if) (2) The store keeper recorded every item. The auditor could check it later. (so that) (3) The hall emptied in two minutes. It was a loud alarm. (such ... that)
practice.answer: (1) If the rain stops by noon, the inter-house final will be played. (The present form stops follows the time-and-condition subordinator; a comma marks the fronted clause; if the pair is reversed the comma is dropped: The inter-house final will be played if the rain stops by noon.) (2) The store keeper recorded every item so that the auditor could check it later. (No comma is needed before a second-position purpose clause; so that must appear whole.) (3) It was such a loud alarm that the hall emptied in two minutes. (such a + adjective + noun, then the that-clause of result.)

marking.criterion: (1) both ideas subordinated with if, no fragment
(1) comma after the fronted clause (or none, correctly, after reversal) and present form after if
(2) purpose joined with the whole subordinator so that
(3) result that-clause completes the sentence with no comma splice

practice.question: Correct each of the following, which is a fragment, a comma splice or a wrong verb form, and say what was wrong. (1) Because the generators failed twice. (2) It was raining, we cancelled the trip. (3) I will call you as soon as you will arrive.
practice.answer: (1) Fragment: the because-clause has no main clause. Attach one - Because the generators failed twice, the demonstration continued. (2) Comma splice: two main clauses are joined by a comma alone. Subordinate one - Because it was raining, we cancelled the trip - or coordinate them - It was raining, so we cancelled the trip. (3) Wrong form after a time subordinator: will is not used in the as soon as clause. Correct - I will call you as soon as you arrive.

marking.criterion: (1) named as a fragment (no main clause)
(2) named as a comma splice (two main clauses, comma alone)
(3) corrected to a present form after as soon as
(3) reason given: a time subordinator takes a present or perfect form, not will

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: The eight diphthongs: definition, spellings, accent variation and checked examples
objectives: Define a diphthong as one vowel sound that glides in quality within a single syllable, and tell it from a pure vowel and from the number of vowel letters in the spelling.
Name the eight diphthongs of the British teaching model in one consistent IPA set and state the accent the set belongs to.
Give two dictionary-checked example words for each diphthong with their usual spellings and some spelling variants, without treating spelling as a guide to sound.
Use pronunciation-dictionary entries to correct words placed under the wrong diphthong (brought, faults, Nassau, pear, poor, sure) and handle words with two accepted pronunciations (either, tour).
Describe the main differences between the UK and US dictionary entries for these sounds.
Complete a keyed, marked exercise, including two checked examples of each diphthong.
lessons.body:
A diphthong is a single vowel sound whose quality changes while it is being said: the tongue and lips start in one vowel position and glide towards another, all within one syllable. In day, the sound begins at a mid vowel and moves towards /ɪ/, yet you hear one vowel, not two. A pure vowel such as /iː/ in see keeps one steady quality from start to finish. Be careful with spelling: the spelling oy in boy represents a diphthong, while ea in beat represents a pure vowel. The test is always the sound a speaker produces, never the number of letters.
This lesson extends the earlier lesson on sound symbols and uses the same British reference model, shown in the UK entries of the Cambridge Dictionary. It does not claim that every accent of English has the same sounds. The eight diphthongs of this model are /eɪ/, /əʊ/, /aɪ/, /aʊ/, /ɔɪ/, /ɪə/, /eə/ and /ʊə/. If a list you have seen shows only seven, the missing one is /əʊ/. The first five end in a glide towards /ɪ/ or /ʊ/. The last three, /ɪə/, /eə/ and /ʊə/, end in a glide towards the central vowel /ə/. British dictionary entries may show an optional r after a vowel, as in here /hɪə(r)/; that /r/ is spoken only when a vowel follows. This lesson writes each diphthong without it.
Accents differ, and the dictionary shows it. The Cambridge US entries write /oʊ/ where the UK entries write /əʊ/ (go: UK /ɡəʊ/, US /ɡoʊ/). For the words here, care and tour, the US entries use a vowel followed by /r/ (here /hɪr/, care /ker/, tour /tʊr/) rather than the UK centring diphthongs. This is not a rule that every UK centring diphthong becomes a vowel plus /r/: idea has US /aɪˈdiː.ə/, with no /r/. Even inside the UK entries a word can have two forms, as tour does. So the eight-diphthong chart is a teaching convention for one model, not a fact about all English speech, and a learner should always say which model is being used.
/eɪ/ is the vowel of day /deɪ/ and plate /pleɪt/. It is spelled ay in day and a…e in plate (a, one consonant, then a silent e). It is also spelled ea in great, which the dictionary shows as /ɡreɪt/. Other spellings of /eɪ/ exist, but check any new word before using it as an example, because the same letters stand for different sounds in different words.
/əʊ/ is the vowel of go /ɡəʊ/ and boat /bəʊt/. It is spelled o in go, oa in boat and ow in grow /ɡrəʊ/. The US entries write it /oʊ/ (go /ɡoʊ/, boat /boʊt/); that is a difference of accent, not of word. Do not describe this sound as “the long o”: that names a letter, not a sound. Do not confuse /əʊ/ with /aʊ/: grow and now both end in ow, but grow has /əʊ/ and now has /aʊ/.
/aɪ/ is the vowel of sky /skaɪ/ and height /haɪt/. It is spelled y in sky and eigh in height; the dictionary itself uses the word eye as its key word for this sound. Either has two accepted pronunciations: the UK entry lists /ˈaɪðə(r)/ and /ˈiːðə(r)/, and the US entry lists the two the other way round. It is therefore not a safe fixed example of /aɪ/; if you use it, say which pronunciation you mean.
/aʊ/ is the vowel of now /naʊ/ and about /əˈbaʊt/. It is spelled ow in now and ou in about. Spelling is not a safe guide: Nassau, the capital of the Bahamas, looks as if it contains /aʊ/, but the dictionary shows /ˈnæsɔː/, which ends in /ɔː/.
/ɔɪ/ is the vowel of boy /bɔɪ/ and noise /nɔɪz/. It is spelled oy in boy and oi in noise. Write the first symbol as the open-o /ɔ/, not with a capital or Cyrillic look-alike.
/ɪə/ is the vowel of here /hɪə(r)/ and idea /aɪˈdɪə/. It is spelled ere in here and ea in idea. The US entries do not use a diphthong here: here is /hɪr/ and idea is /aɪˈdiːə/, with two syllables after /aɪ/. Pear is not an example of /ɪə/: its UK entry is /peə(r)/, which has the next diphthong.
/eə/ is the vowel of care /keə(r)/ and heir /eə(r)/. It is spelled are in care and eir in heir. Air /eə(r)/ and wear /weə(r)/ show two more spellings, air and ear, and pear /peə(r)/ has the same vowel and spelling pattern as wear. In the US entries these words use /e/ followed by /r/ (care /ker/, heir /er/).
/ʊə/ is the vowel of pure /pjʊə(r)/ and tour /tʊə(r)/. It is spelled ure in pure and our in tour. It is the least stable of the eight. The UK entry for tour lists /tɔː(r)/ as well as /tʊə(r)/, and the UK entries for poor and sure show /pɔː(r)/ and /ʃɔː(r)/, with /ɔː/ and not /ʊə/, so poor and sure are not examples of /ʊə/ in this model. The US entries use /ʊ/ followed by /r/ (pure /pjʊr/, tour /tʊr/, poor /pʊr/).
Some class lists put words under the wrong sound. Check these against the UK entries: brought is /brɔːt/, not /eɪ/; fault is /fɒlt/, so faults is not an /əʊ/ word; Nassau is /ˈnæsɔː/, not /aʊ/; pear is /peə(r)/, not /ɪə/. Four spelling labels also need correcting from the spelling alone: hoe and foe are spelled oe, grow and thrown are spelled ow, eye is spelled eye, and air, fair and hair are spelled air.
To check a word, find its UK entry, read the vowel symbol between the consonants and match it to the eight above; then look at the US entry to see whether the accent changes the vowel. When you are asked for two examples of a diphthong, give two words whose entries you have checked, not words that only look similar. This lesson teaches symbol recognition from written dictionary entries. It does not test or certify how you say the sounds: listening to an authorised model and the teacher’s oral observation remain separate.

practice.question: Write the symbol of the diphthong in each word, using the British model of this lesson: day, go, sky, about, boy, idea, heir, tour.
practice.answer: day /eɪ/; go /əʊ/; sky /aɪ/; about /aʊ/; boy /ɔɪ/; idea /ɪə/; heir /eə/; tour /ʊə/ in the teaching model; also accept /ɔː/ if the learner identifies the alternative UK pronunciation, noting that this alternative is a pure vowel rather than a diphthong.

practice.question: Define a diphthong in one sentence and give one reason why the number of vowel letters in a word cannot tell you whether it has one.
practice.answer: A diphthong is one vowel sound that glides from one quality to another within a single syllable. The number of letters cannot decide it because spelling does not match sound: oy in boy represents a diphthong, whereas ea in beat represents a pure vowel.

marking.criterion: one vowel sound that changes quality (glides)
a reason or a contrasting pair showing that letters do not decide the sound

practice.question: Write the letters that spell the diphthong in each word: height, heir, idea.
practice.answer: height: eigh; heir: eir; idea: ea.

practice.question: A class list shows brought under /eɪ/, pear under /ɪə/ and Nassau under /aʊ/. For each word, say which vowel the Cambridge UK entry shows.
practice.answer: brought: /ɔː/, so it is not an /eɪ/ word. pear: /eə/, so it is not an /ɪə/ word. Nassau: /ɔː/ in its last syllable, so it is not an /aʊ/ word.

practice.question: Write two examples of each of the eight diphthongs: /eɪ/, /əʊ/, /aɪ/, /aʊ/, /ɔɪ/, /ɪə/, /eə/, /ʊə/. Use words whose Cambridge UK entries you have checked.
practice.answer: Model answer: /eɪ/ day, plate; /əʊ/ go, boat; /aɪ/ sky, height; /aʊ/ now, about; /ɔɪ/ boy, noise; /ɪə/ here, idea; /eə/ care, heir; /ʊə/ pure, tour. Accept any other word whose UK entry shows the target diphthong, for example great /ɡreɪt/ under /eɪ/, or air /eə(r)/ and wear /weə(r)/ under /eə/. Do not accept poor, sure, brought, faults, Nassau or pear under the diphthongs this lesson rejects them for; a word repeated within the same diphthong counts once; a US-only form does not count for /ɪə/, /eə/ or /ʊə/.

practice.question: (a) Write the Cambridge US transcription of go and of care. (b) Does every word with a UK centring diphthong acquire /r/ in the US entry? Use idea as evidence.
practice.answer: (a) go /ɡoʊ/; care /ker/. (b) No. Cambridge gives US idea as /aɪˈdiː.ə/, with no /r/.

marking.criterion: No, supported by the US transcription of idea without /r/.

lessons.subject: English Language
lessons.title: Revision: matching the single vowel sounds /æ/, /ɪ/, /iː/, /ʌ/ and /ɔː/
objectives: Match words by vowel sound from the bracketed letters, not by spelling.
Identify the vowels /æ/, /ɪ/, /iː/, /ʌ/ and /ɔː/ and give key words for each.
Recognise the common spellings of each sound and the traps where the same letters stand for different sounds.
Distinguish the confusable pairs /ɪ/ and /iː/, /æ/ and /e/, /ʌ/ and /ʊ/, /ʌ/ and /ɑː/, /ɔː/ and /ɒ/, and /ɔː/ and /ɜː/.
State the accent model, and accept a stated variant such as the sounded r or the vowel of bath.
Answer a keyed, marked revision set and explain each key by the sounds of the options.
lessons.body:
This is a revision set on one skill: matching words by vowel sound when the target letters are shown in square brackets. It is built from the five Week 6 revision questions, which ask for the word with the same vowel sound as the letters underlined in the stem. The five stems test five different single vowel sounds, /æ/, /ɪ/, /iː/, /ʌ/ and /ɔː/, so they belong to the single-vowel teaching of Week 3 and not to the diphthongs that Week 6 teaches; this lesson is therefore labelled as revision and does not claim to assess the Week 6 scheme objectives. The source gives no key, its underlining appears only in the stems and is lost in the extracted text, and its options carry no marking of which letters count, so no answer is inferred from the options. Every word, item and answer below is newly written, and the square brackets do the work that the underline did in the source.
In a matching question the sound is the unit, not the spelling. First say the bracketed letters inside the whole word and listen for the vowel; then write its symbol; then test every option in the same way. Two words match when their stressed vowels are the same phoneme, even if the spellings are completely different. Two words with the same letters do not match if their vowels differ. The brackets may include letters that are not vowel letters: in north the bracketed letters are or, yet in the British model only the vowel /ɔː/ is heard, because an r before a consonant is not pronounced. Always match the vowel sound, not the number or the kind of letters.
The five sounds, each with key words, are these. /æ/ is the short vowel of cat, hand, lamp and glad, made with the jaw open. /ɪ/ is the short vowel of sit, gift and six, made with relaxed lips. /iː/ is the long vowel of see, team and key, made with spread lips. /ʌ/ is the short vowel of cup, sun and love, made with the mouth relaxed and open. /ɔː/ is the long vowel of saw, tall, corn and north, made with rounded lips. The length mark is part of the symbol: /iː/ and /ɔː/ are long, while /æ/, /ɪ/ and /ʌ/ are short. All five are monophthongs, so the vowel is held steady and does not glide as the diphthongs of the Week 6 teaching do.
Each sound has several common spellings. /æ/ is almost always written a, as in clap and sad. /ɪ/ is written i in sit and six, but also y in gym, u in busy, o in women and ui in build. /iː/ is written ee in see, ea in team, ey in key, ie in field, ei in seize and e in these. /ʌ/ is written u in cup and sun, o in come, son and love, ou in couple and young, and oo in blood. /ɔː/ is written or in fork and corn, aw in saw, a before ll in ball and wall, augh in caught, ough in thought, oor in door, and ar after w in warm. A learner who knows only the first spelling of each sound will miss many correct answers.
The same letters can stand for different vowels, which is why spelling cannot be used to choose an answer. The letters ea are /iː/ in team, /e/ in head and /eɪ/ in great. The letter u is /ʌ/ in cup, /ʊ/ in put and /ɪ/ in busy. The letter o is /ʌ/ in love, /uː/ in move, /əʊ/ in home and /ʊ/ in woman, but /ɪ/ in women. The letters oo are /ʌ/ in blood, /uː/ in food and /ʊ/ in book. In a well-made matching item the wrong options often look like the stem or like the right answer, so a word that looks right is exactly the word to check by sound.
Six contrasts cause most errors. /ɪ/ and /iː/ differ in length and quality: sit and seat are different words. /æ/ and /e/ differ in the height of the tongue and the opening of the jaw: bad and bed. /ʌ/ and /ʊ/ are both short and are often both written u: cut has /ʌ/ and put has /ʊ/, with rounder lips. /ʌ/ and /ɑː/ differ in length and position: cut and cart. /ɔː/ and /ɒ/ differ in length and rounding: caught and cot. /ɔː/ and /ɜː/ are both long vowels that are often written with or: north has /ɔː/, but worth has /ɜː/. When two options seem to match, test these contrasts first.
This lesson uses one model: British English as shown by a British pronunciation dictionary, with the symbol set of the earlier lessons. Accent matters in some words. In British English an r written after a vowel and before a consonant, or at the end of a word, is not pronounced, so north is /nɔːθ/ and car is /kɑː/; in American English the r is sounded, as in /nɔːrθ/ and /kɑːr/, and the vowel being matched is the same one with an r added. A few words change their vowel instead: bath has /ɑː/ in British English and /æ/ in American English, and top has /ɒ/ in British English and often /ɑː/ in American English. A fair item therefore uses words whose vowel is the same in both models, or states its accent in the key. The matching items in Q1 to Q3 use such words; Q6 uses bath on purpose, to practise stating an accent. A stated accent variant is correct when the key accepts it.
Use a fixed method for a matching item. First, read the stem and say the bracketed letters inside the word. Second, write the vowel symbol beside the stem. Third, say each option with its own bracketed letters and write its symbol. Fourth, choose the option whose symbol is identical, including the length mark. Fifth, if two options seem to match, check length first (/ɪ/ against /iː/), then the lips (/ʌ/ against /ʊ/ and /ɔː/), then accent. Sixth, do not choose an option because it contains the same letters or because it rhymes with the stem. A good key shows the stem symbol and each option’s symbol, as the keys below do, so that a wrong choice can be traced to the sound that was misheard.
Written matching shows that a learner can name sounds and ignore spelling. It does not by itself prove that the mouth makes the contrast reliably, and no written key can certify listening or speaking; pronunciation is assessed by oral observation with an authorised model, which is outside this written lesson. The practice below has six exercises of ten marks each, sixty marks in all: matching with four options A to D and exactly one correct option, naming the vowel, finding the odd one out, giving examples, correcting false rules and stating accent. Every item is original. The five parts of Q1 test the five sounds once each, and Q2 to Q5 revisit them from different directions.

practice.question: Choose the word, A to D, that has the same vowel sound as the letters in square brackets, and write the vowel symbol. (a) gl[a]d: A. p[a]ge B. l[a]mp C. c[a]r D. t[a]ll. (b) b[u]sy: A. b[u]s B. b[u]sh C. s[i]t D. s[ee]d. (c) k[ey]: A. gr[ey] B. h[ea]d C. t[ea]m D. s[i]x. (d) c[o]me: A. h[o]me B. l[o]ve C. m[o]ve D. w[o]man. (e) n[or]th: A. w[or]se B. c[or]n C. t[o]p D. f[ir]st.
practice.answer: (a) B, /æ/: glad and lamp both have /æ/; page is /eɪ/, car is /ɑː/ and tall is /ɔː/. (b) C, /ɪ/: the u in busy is /ɪ/ and sit has /ɪ/; bus is /ʌ/, bush is /ʊ/ and seed is /iː/. (c) C, /iː/: key and team both have /iː/; grey is /eɪ/, head is /e/ and six is /ɪ/. (d) B, /ʌ/: come and love both have /ʌ/; home is /əʊ/, move is /uː/ and woman is /ʊ/. (e) B, /ɔː/: north and corn both have /ɔː/ (an r is sounded after the vowel in American English); worse and first are /ɜː/, and top is /ɒ/ in British English. One mark for the option and one for the symbol in each part.

practice.question: Write the symbol of the vowel sound in the bracketed letters of each word, choosing from /æ ɪ iː ʌ ɔː/. (a) cl[a]p (b) w[o]men (c) f[ie]ld (d) bl[oo]d (e) w[a]ll.
practice.answer: (a) /æ/. (b) /ɪ/: the o in women is /ɪ/. (c) /iː/: ie is /iː/ in field. (d) /ʌ/: oo is /ʌ/ in blood, unlike food. (e) /ɔː/: a before ll is /ɔː/ in wall. The length mark must be written for /iː/ and /ɔː/; a symbol without it earns no mark.

practice.question: In each set, one word has a different vowel sound in the bracketed letters. Write the odd word and the symbol of the vowel shared by the other three. (a) s[ea]t, k[ey], h[ea]d, f[ie]ld. (b) l[o]ve, s[u]n, c[ou]ple, p[u]t. (c) c[a]t, h[a]nd, p[a]ge, s[a]d. (d) f[or]k, s[aw], b[a]ll, w[or]se. (e) s[i]t, b[u]sy, g[i]ft, p[ee]l.
practice.answer: (a) head: the others share /iː/; head has /e/. (b) put: the others share /ʌ/; put has /ʊ/. (c) page: the others share /æ/; page has /eɪ/. (d) worse: the others share /ɔː/; worse has /ɜː/. (e) peel: the others share /ɪ/; peel has /iː/. One mark for the odd word and one for the shared symbol in each set.

practice.question: Give two different words for each of the five sounds /æ/, /ɪ/, /iː/, /ʌ/ and /ɔː/. Do not use a word that appears in Q1 to Q3. Show the target letters in square brackets.
practice.answer: One model set, with other correct words accepted: /æ/ b[a]g, m[a]n; /ɪ/ p[i]n, b[i]g; /iː/ s[ee], m[ea]l; /ʌ/ c[u]p, s[o]n; /ɔː/ d[oo]r, p[or]t. Award one mark for each word whose stressed vowel is the named sound in the British model, with the target letters bracketed. Accept a word whose only difference from the British vowel is a sounded r in American English, as in door and port. Do not accept a word that shares only the spelling, such as head for /iː/, and do not accept the same word twice or a word with an accent-dependent vowel, such as bath for /æ/, unless the accent is stated.

practice.question: Each statement is false. Correct it and give one word as evidence. (a) The letters ea always stand for /iː/. (b) The letter u is always /ʌ/. (c) The sound /ɔː/ is always spelt or. (d) Sit and seat have the same vowel because the second differs only in spelling. (e) Words that end in the same letters always rhyme.
practice.answer: (a) ea can also be /e/ or /eɪ/: head has /e/ and great has /eɪ/. (b) u can be /ʊ/ or /ɪ/ as well: put has /ʊ/ and busy has /ɪ/. (c) /ɔː/ is also written aw, a before ll, augh and ough: saw and wall. (d) The vowels differ in length and quality: sit has /ɪ/ and seat has /iː/. (e) Spelling does not decide rhyme: love and move end in the same letters, but love has /ʌ/ and move has /uː/. One mark for the correction and one for the evidence in each part; any correct word of the same kind earns the evidence mark.

practice.question: For each word, write the British vowel symbol and say whether the American vowel differs. (a) b[a]th (b) n[or]th (c) c[a]r (d) gl[a]d (e) c[o]me.
practice.answer: (a) British /ɑː/; American /æ/, so the vowel differs; either vowel is acceptable only if the accent is named. (b) British /ɔː/; American has the same vowel with the r sounded, /ɔːr/, so the vowel quality is the same. (c) British /ɑː/; American has the same vowel with the r sounded, /ɑːr/, so the vowel quality is the same. (d) /æ/ in both. (e) /ʌ/ in both. One mark for the British symbol and one for the correct comparison in each part.

marking.criterion: (b) /ɔː/ and same vowel with sounded r
(c) /ɑː/ and same vowel with sounded r

evidence.locator: SUP-SS1-ENGLISH-MONOPHTHONGS-T1: body paragraph 1

evidence.locator: SUP-SS1-ENGLISH-ADVERBIAL-CLAUSE-T1: body paragraphs 1 to 9 and practice Q1 to Q4
evidence.explanation: Teaches the adverbial clause itself: paragraph 1 defines it as a subordinate clause performing the adverbial function and gives the two identification tests (own subject plus finite verb inside the group; movable or removable as an adverbial); paragraph 2 names the subordinators and requires classification from the relation, not from the isolated word (since, as and that each do more than one job); paragraph 3 separates an adverbial clause from an adverbial phrase and from a noun clause; paragraph 4 gives punctuation - comma after a fronted clause, none when the clause follows the main clause - and the fragment and comma-splice errors, including the so against so that distinction; paragraphs 5 to 8 teach the eight kinds the objective names, one clear original example each: time (When the bell rang, the pupils carried their exercise books to the staff room) with the present-for-future rule after a time subordinator, place (Where the path leaves the main road, a broken signpost still points to the health centre), reason (The practical was cancelled because the laboratory had no water), purpose (The teacher repeated the instruction twice so that no pupil would miss it), condition (If the school bus starts by seven, the team will reach the venue before the practical begins) with unless meaning if ... not, concession (Although the generators failed twice, the demonstration continued), result (The queue was so long that the bell rang before Tunde reached the desk) with the so/such ... that frame, and manner (The trainee nurse held the bottle as her instructor had shown her; as if and as though). Paragraph 9 gives the four-step method and a worked example. Practice Q1 identifies and classifies six clauses (12 marks), Q2 separates clause from phrase (8 marks), Q3 combines pairs with a given subordinator under correct punctuation (6 marks) and Q4 corrects a fragment, a comma splice and a wrong verb form (6 marks): 32 marks, all keyed. Bound additively: no correction is created, displaced or amended, the source body rows for Week 6 are untouched, and the Week 10 adverbial-phrase objective ENGLISH-BODY-034 is not claimed by this row and does not claim this one. The grammatical descriptions were checked against the Cambridge Dictionary English Grammar sections named in provenance entry 2, read 2026-11-06; the place label is flagged for owner review in provenance entry 3, as is whether Week 6 should carry the objective at all, which the scheme row alone evidences.
